title: Weekly Reflections
text:
AI and originality
This week, I learned how AI can enhance learning without replacing original thought. AI is beneficial for me when used as a support tool for understanding concepts, while originality comes from how ideas are interpreted and communicated by me. I use AI to help me study! For example,it is beneficial for me to break down difficult concepts so that I can understand them in more simple terms and real-world scenario examples.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: What is AGI? How does AGI affect scientific research?
text:
What is AGI? How does AGI affect scientific research?
I learned that Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) refers to systems capable of performing human level tasks. AGI could help enhance scientific research through faster data analysis, but it also causes ethical concerns in regards to responsible use.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: How do humans find knowledge? How is knowledge different from information?
text:
How do humans find knowledge? How is knowledge different from information?
People find knowledge by noticing patterns in information and linking them to what they already understand. Information is data that has been organized, but knowledge is when you understand the reasons behind things and how they connect. When we mine for knowledge, we look for useful patterns and remove what is not important.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: List of AI discrepancies/failures. Any pattern?
text:
List of AI discrepancies/failures. Any pattern?
AI systems can make errors such as generating fabricated information, perpetuating biases, or identifying patterns that lack significance. These issues arise when AI models detect patterns without understanding their meaning. The primary challenge is that AI may mistake genuine knowledge for random or biased data.

title: Weekly Reflections
text:
Start your first ML pipeline.
For my first ML pipeline, I used my healthcare claims Web Description dataset. I cleaned the claim text, created text-based features, split the data into training and testing sets, and used a logistic regression model to predict whether a claim was high impact or lower impact.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: What did the error analysis reveal that the accuracy score alone did not? How does overfitting relate to knowledge vs. noise?
text:
What did the error analysis reveal that the accuracy score alone did not? How does overfitting relate to knowledge vs. noise?
The accuracy score only showed how often the model was correct overall. The error analysis showed which specific claim descriptions the model got wrong, which helped explain where the model was confused.
Overfitting happens when a model memorizes the training data instead of learning useful patterns. This means the model may be learning noise instead of real knowledge, so checking test accuracy is important.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: Prediction vs. explanation: when does it matter why something happens, and when is it enough to know what will happen? Give a policy or research example.
text:
Prediction vs. explanation: when does it matter why something happens, and when is it enough to know what will happen? Give a policy or research example.
Prediction helps us see what might happen, like which neighborhoods could face high eviction rates next year. Explanation is needed when we want to fix the problem. We need to know why evictions happen to make good policies. For example, a model might predict eviction based on rent debt, but we also need to check if job loss, higher rents, or weak tenant protections are causing it. If we only look at predictions, we might act too late or choose solutions that do not work.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: Draw a simple causal diagram for a relationship in your research area. What confounders exist? How would you distinguish a causal claim from a predictive association?
text:
Draw a simple causal diagram for a relationship in your research area. What confounders exist? How would you distinguish a causal claim from a predictive association?
A simple causal diagram is: education level affects income. Confounders are things like family background, neighborhood, school quality, and work experience. These can change both education and income. A causal claim says education changes income. A predictive association just means the two are linked. To tell the difference, I would use experiments or control for confounders with statistics.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: How can text mining reveal patterns that close reading alone cannot? What are its blind spots?
text:
How can text mining reveal patterns that close reading alone cannot? What are its blind spots?
Text mining lets us look at lots of documents quickly. It finds common words, themes, and trends. Close reading gives more detail but is too slow for big collections. Text mining can miss sarcasm, tone, or hidden meaning. It can also make common words seem more important than they are.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: How NLP and LLM can assist in your research and provide data/assistance for your project? Give specific examples.
text:
How NLP and LLM can assist in your research and provide data/assistance for your project? Give specific examples.
Natural language processing helps clean text, find key terms, and spot common topics. It can also compare documents over time. Large language models can summarize long reports, suggest coding ideas, and explain patterns in simple words. For example, in a job-posting project, NLP can count how often skills like data analysis or policy appear. An LLM can group similar job descriptions. In a defense report project, these tools can track changes in words about strategy, risk, or threats.

title: Weekly Reflections
text:
Name limitations and suggest solutions.
One problem is bias in the data, which can lead to unfair results. Another is hallucination, where the model gives wrong information but sounds sure. Loss of context is also an issue, especially in short summaries. To fix these, we need to check outputs by hand, use trusted sources, report uncertainty, and keep humans involved.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: Write an AI for research guide (you can use bullet points) incorporating ethical, technical and academic concerns that could lead to more problems than solutions (e.g. Hinton).
text:
Write an AI for research guide (you can use bullet points) incorporating ethical, technical and academic concerns that could lead to more problems than solutions (e.g. Hinton).

Use AI to support research, not replace human judgment.
Always verify facts, quotes, and citations with original sources.
Do not paste private, sensitive, or protected data into AI tools.
Report when AI was used and explain how it was used.
Watch for bias, hallucinations, and weak reasoning before trusting results.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: What can LLMs do well, and where do they fail? Evaluate one specific failure mode (hallucination, bias, reasoning error) you have encountered.
text:
What can LLMs do well, and where do they fail? Evaluate one specific failure mode (hallucination, bias, reasoning error) you have encountered.
Large language models are good at summarizing, giving ideas, rewriting text, and explaining hard topics in simple words. They are not as good when they give wrong information but sound confident. I have seen hallucination, where the model makes up sources or details that are not in the data. This is risky in research because false information can look true if it is written clearly.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: How might generative AI reshape your discipline in the next five years? What research tasks will change most, and what should remain human-driven?
text:
How might generative AI reshape your discipline in the next five years? What research tasks will change most, and what should remain human-driven?
Generative AI will likely speed up research by helping with coding, summarizing, drafting, and text analysis. Literature reviews, first drafts, and sorting documents will change the most. But humans should still choose research questions, pick theories, handle ethics, and explain results. Researchers also need to check for accuracy, fairness, and real-world effects.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and why does it matter for research? How does grounding generation in retrieved documents change the trustworthiness of AI output?
text:
What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and why does it matter for research? How does grounding generation in retrieved documents change the trustworthiness of AI output?
Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, is when an AI system uses outside documents or sources before creating an answer. This matters for research because the response is not only based on what the AI already knows. Instead, it is connected to information that can be checked.
Grounding the answer in retrieved documents can make AI output more trustworthy because the response is supported by actual sources. This helps reduce made-up information and makes it easier to verify where the answer came from. However, the answer still depends on the quality of the documents and whether the AI uses them correctly.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: What are the recent criticisms about RAG? Any suggestions for improving generation?
text:
What are the recent criticisms about RAG? Any suggestions for improving generation?
One criticism of RAG is that it can still give inaccurate answers if it retrieves the wrong documents or misunderstands the information. Another issue is that users may trust the answer too much just because it looks source-based, even when the sources are weak or not fully relevant.
To improve generation, RAG systems should use better source selection, stronger filtering, and clearer citations. The AI should also check whether the retrieved documents actually answer the question before generating a response. Overall, RAG is useful for research, but it should still be reviewed by humans to make sure the final answer is accurate and reliable.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: What is a knowledge graph and how does it differ from a traditional database or a vector store? Why are relationships between entities valuable for knowledge mining?
text:
What is a knowledge graph and how does it differ from a traditional database or a vector store? Why are relationships between entities valuable for knowledge mining?
A knowledge graph organizes information by showing how things are connected. A traditional database usually stores data in tables, and a vector store helps find information based on similarity. A knowledge graph is different because it focuses more on relationships and meaning.
Relationships are useful for knowledge mining because they help explain patterns in the data. For example, in our project, we are not just looking at confidence in banks by itself. We are looking at how confidence connects to income, education, age, and survey year using GSS data and a Shiny app.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: Identify three entities and three relationships from your research domain that could form a small knowledge graph. How would this structure help answer questions that a flat dataset cannot?
text:
Identify three entities and three relationships from your research domain that could form a small knowledge graph. How would this structure help answer questions that a flat dataset cannot?
Three entities from my research domain could be income group, survey year, and confidence in banks. Three relationships could be: income group is associated with confidence in banks, survey year affects confidence patterns, and post-2008 years are linked to lower confidence in banks.
This structure would help answer deeper questions because it shows how the variables connect instead of only listing them in a table. A flat dataset can show the numbers, but a knowledge graph can make the relationships easier to follow. For example, it could show that income differences exist but are small, while survey year has a stronger connection to confidence in banks.

title: Weekly Reflections
section: What does “AI for Science” mean? How do agentic AI systems change the research workflow compared to single-prompt interactions?
text:
What does “AI for Science” mean? How do agentic AI systems change the research workflow compared to single-prompt interactions?
“AI for Science” means using AI to support the research process. This can include finding patterns in data, helping with coding, summarizing results, checking statistical output, or explaining findings in a clearer way. In research, AI is useful because it can speed up parts of the process, but the researcher still has to review the results and make sure they are accurate.
Agentic AI systems are different from single-prompt interactions because they can plan steps, use tools, and work through a task in stages. A single prompt usually gives one answer at one time. An agentic system can do more, such as clean data, run a model, create charts, compare results, and revise the output based on what it finds.
This changes the research workflow because AI becomes more like a research assistant instead of just a writing tool. However, it still needs human oversight because AI can misunderstand data, overstate findings, or make unsupported conclusions. The best use is to let AI support the workflow while the researcher stays responsible for the final analysis.

title: Assignment 2 – Prompt Exercise
text: This assignment shows how different AI models respond to the same research task. The goal is to design prompts, evaluate model outputs, refine instructions, and understand how prompt structure impacts response quality.

title: Assignment 2 – Prompt Exercise
text: This assignment shows how different AI models respond to the same research task. The goal is to design prompts, evaluate model outputs, refine instructions, and understand how prompt structure impacts response quality.

title: Assignment 2 – Prompt Exercise
text:
Design Prompt
For the first test, I submitted the following prompt to multiple AI models:
Write a 1,500 word literature review that reads like an analytical discussion rather than a textbook summary. Start by explaining the purpose and scope of the review. Include a methodology section describing how ideas, themes, and findings are compared across studies. Add key insights by identifying patterns, similarities, and differences. Highlight important trends, challenges, and meaningful research gaps. Finish by suggesting one realistic and testable hypothesis that logically follows from the discussion. Maintain a formal but clear writing style, prioritizing explanation and reasoning over definitions or lists.
The prompt was submitted to ChatGPT, Copilot, and Grok 3.

title: Assignment 2 – Prompt Exercise
text:
Model Response Analysis
Each model response was evaluated using the following criteria:
Structure
Did it include a methodology section and follow a systematic review format?
Synthesis
Were key findings from data mining and machine learning applications well-summarized?
Trends and Gaps
Did it identify meaningful trends and research gaps?
Hypothesis Quality
Was the proposed hypothesis testable and relevant?
References
Are the citations accurate (check using Google Scholar or Semantic Scholar)

title: Assignment 2 – Prompt Exercise
text:
Analyze Model Responses
Structure
Regarding the structure, ChatGPT did a great job because it included a specific section explaining its methodology and followed a professional format. Copilot was also very organized and used clear headings that made the report easy to navigate. Grok 3 included a methodology paragraph as well, but the overall response felt more like one long essay rather than a structured review with clear sections.
Synthesis
When it comes to summarizing data mining and machine learning, ChatGPT was the only model that successfully stayed on topic. It explained how researchers are trying to balance making models accurate while also making them easy for humans to understand. Copilot completely missed the mark here because it wrote about technology in classrooms instead of data mining. Grok 3 focused almost entirely on how AI affects jobs and the economy, which was interesting but didn’t cover enough of the technical machine learning details.
Trends and Gaps
All three models tried to identify trends, but ChatGPT was the most relevant to the prompt by pointing out that researchers are moving away from simple predictions and looking for deeper causes. Copilot identified gaps in how technology affects different students, which was good but for the wrong subject. Grok 3 identified a very modern trend regarding “agentic AI” and noted that we still don’t have enough long-term data on how these systems behave.
Hypothesis Quality
The hypotheses provided were a bit of a mixed bag. ChatGPT created a strong, testable guess about whether adaptive models work better than static ones over a long period of time. Copilot also wrote a clear hypothesis about student learning, but it wasn’t relevant to the actual assignment topic of data mining. Grok 3 failed this part entirely because the response cut off at the end, so it never actually provided a hypothesis to test.
References
For the references and citations, all of the models struggled. None of them provided a list of specific papers, authors, or links that could be double-checked on Google Scholar or Semantic Scholar. They all spoke about “the literature” in a general way without giving credit to specific researchers, which makes it hard to verify if the information is coming from a real study.
Strengths and Weaknesses
In summary, ChatGPT’s main strength was following the instructions perfectly and staying on the right topic, but its weakness was the lack of real citations. Copilot’s strength was its very clean and easy-to-read structure, but its major weakness was hallucinating the wrong topic for the review. Grok 3’s strength was providing very deep and unique thoughts about current AI trends, but its biggest weakness was being incomplete and cutting off before finishing the task.

title: Assignment 2 – Prompt Exercise
text:
Refined Prompts
After reviewing weaknesses, I revised the prompts.
Refined Prompt for ChatGPT
The biggest problem with ChatGPT’s first answer was that it did not name any real scientists or papers. It spoke in a very general way, which makes it hard to prove the information is true. This new prompt tells ChatGPT that it must include specific names and dates for its sources. It also asks for a bibliography at the end so we can check the work using Google Scholar or Semantic Scholar to make sure the citations are accurate.
New Prompt for ChatGPT:
Write a 1,500-word literature review about data mining and machine learning. You must include real in-text citations from academic studies, such as (Author, Year), to support your points. Include a methodology section that explains how you compared different studies. At the very end, provide a full list of references and one realistic, testable hypothesis that researchers could use for a new study.
Refined Prompt for Microsoft Copilot
Microsoft Copilot failed the first time because it wrote about the wrong topic, focusing on education instead of computer science. To fix this, the new prompt uses very strict instructions to stay on the subject of data mining and machine learning. Since Copilot is good at making things look neat, the prompt asks for a clear structure with specific sections for trends and gaps. This will help the model stay focused on the technical requirements of the assignment.
New Prompt for Copilot:
Write an analytical literature review of exactly 1,500 words about the technical applications of Data Mining and Machine Learning. Do not write about “human learning” or “education”; you must focus only on computer science topics like algorithm performance and data patterns. Organize the review with clear sections for methodology, key findings, and research gaps. End the discussion with a formal, testable hypothesis.
Refined Prompt for Grok 3
Grok 3’s first response was smart, but it was too short and it cut off before it could finish the job. It also focused too much on jobs and money instead of the actual technology. The new prompt tells Grok 3 to act like a data scientist and write a much longer review. It also tells the model to balance its time better so that it does not stop talking before it gets to the hypothesis at the very end.
New Prompt for Grok 3:
Imagine you are a data scientist writing a 2,000-word systematic literature review on data mining and machine learning in fields like healthcare and finance. You must provide a clear methodology and focus on the technical side of how models work, such as their accuracy and how they handle complex data. Ensure you manage the length of your response so it is complete. You must finish with a bold and testable hypothesis and a final conclusion.

title: Assignment 2 – Prompt Exercise
text:
Final Prompt
After testing the new prompts, the results were much better because each AI finally followed the specific rules it missed the first time. ChatGPT became more trustworthy by adding real names and dates of scientists to support its ideas, while Copilot finally stopped talking about the wrong topic and stayed focused only on computer science. Grok 3 also did a better job by finishing its entire report and providing a smart “science guess” or hypothesis at the end instead of cutting off early. This shows that when you give an AI very clear instructions and fix its past mistakes, it can write a much more professional and complete paper for your project.
After collecting revised outputs, I used this synthesis prompt:
I am giving you three different drafts for a literature review on Data Mining and Machine Learning. Please combine them into one final 2,000-word systematic review. Use the real-world citations and the methodology from the first draft, the clear headings and organization from the second draft, and the modern technical insights from the third draft. Make sure the final document flows smoothly, maintains a formal tone, and ends with the most realistic and testable hypothesis. [I insert the three model outputs here.]

title: Assignment 2 – Prompt Exercise
text:
Reflection
How did the models respond differently?
Each model handled the systematic review in a different way. ChatGPT focused on the technical history and professional structure of data mining, making sure to connect old methods with new ones. Microsoft Copilot focused more on the layout and organization of the report, though it struggled to stay on the correct topic at the beginning. Grok 3 focused on the newest trends and how AI affects the real world right now, but it had a hard time finishing long responses and often stopped before the end.
Which refinements worked best?
The prompt refinements that worked best were the ones that added very specific requirements. For ChatGPT, telling it to include real-world citations with authors and dates made the review much more accurate. For Copilot, the most helpful change was using bold instructions to stay strictly on the topic of computer science so it wouldn’t talk about other subjects. For Grok 3, the best fix was asking it to be more concise and watch its length, which helped it complete the final sections and the hypothesis.
What did this exercise demonstrate?
I learned that using AI for academic reviews requires a lot of back-and-forth work to get a good result. You cannot just use the first answer the AI gives you; you have to check for missing parts and fix the instructions to get better details. I also learned that it is best to use multiple models because one might be better at organizing while another is better at finding modern trends. The most important lesson is that a human must guide the AI and verify all the facts to make sure the final paper is correct and complete.
AI Disclaimer: I used ChatGPT as a tutor to clarify instructions, troubleshoot errors, and better understand mistakes encountered during the process. It also assisted with wording and formatting; however, the final submission reflects my own work and judgment.

For the scatterplot, plot.new() gave me a blank frame and plot.window() set the coordinates, but the actual graph started filling in when the lines() and points() calls ran. The three axis() calls added the bottom, left, and right axes, then box(), mtext(), and text() filled in the border and labels. #
# Comment:
#
# A sophisticated example of adding further output to a basic plot.
#
# Most of the functions defined are just for calculating values
# relevant to the data analysis.
#
# The function plotPars() is the one of interest for seeing how
# the drawing of the plot is done.
#

params <- function(N, breaks, p=seq(0.001, 1, length=100)) {
  list(
    N=N,
    T=1/breaks,
    p=p,
    q=1-p
  )
}

pdfcomp <- function(comp, params) {
  n <- params$T
  p <- params$p
  q <- params$q
  y <- round(comp/n)

  choose(n, comp) * p^comp * q^(n-comp) / (1 - q^n)
}

# Expected num sherds (for a vessel) [=completeness]
expcomp <- function(params) {
  params$T * params$p / (1 - params$q^params$T)
}

# Variance of num sherds (for a vessel)
varcomp <- function(params) {
  n <- params$T
  p <- params$p
  q <- params$q

  # From Johnson & Kotz
  (n*p*q / (1 - q^n)) -
    (n^2*p^2*q^n / (1 - q^n)^2)

  # n^2 times Thomas Yee's formula
  # n^2*((p*(1 + p*(n - 1)) / (n*(1 - q^n))) -
  #       (p^2 / (1 - q^n)^2))
}

# Expected value of completeness (for a sample of vessels)
expmeancomp <- function(params) {
  expcomp(params)
}

# Variance of completeness (for a sample of vessels)
# Use the expected number of vessels in sample as denominator
varmeancomp <- function(params) {
  varcomp(params) / numvess(params)
}

numvess <- function(params) {
  params$N * (1 - params$q^params$T)
}

ecomp <- function(p, T, comp) {
  q <- 1 - p
  T*p / (1 - q^T) - comp
}

estN <- function(comp, broke, n) {
  T <- 1/broke

  n / (
    1 -
      (
        1 -
          uniroot(
            ecomp,
            c(0.00001, 1),
            T=T,
            comp=comp
          )$root
      )^T
  )
}

nvessscale <- function(params, xlim, ylim, new=TRUE) {

  if (new)
    par(new=TRUE)

  plot(
    0:1,
    c(1, params$N),
    type="n",
    axes=!new,
    ann=FALSE,
    xlim=xlim,
    ylim=ylim
  )
}

compscale <- function(params, xlim, ylim, new=TRUE) {

  if (new)
    par(new=TRUE)

  plot(
    0:1,
    c(1, params$T),
    type="n",
    axes=!new,
    ann=FALSE,
    xlim=xlim,
    ylim=ylim
  )
}

lowerCI <- function(p, N, breaks, lb) {

  params <- params(N, breaks, p)

  expmeancomp(params) -
    2*sqrt(varmeancomp(params)) -
    lb
}

upperCI <- function(p, N, breaks, lb) {

  params <- params(N, breaks, p)

  expmeancomp(params) +
    2*sqrt(varmeancomp(params)) -
    lb
}

critP <- function(comp, params) {

  c(
    uniroot(
      lowerCI,
      c(0.00001, 1),
      N=params$N,
      breaks=1/params$T,
      lb=max(comp)
    )$root,

    if (
      upperCI(
        0.00001,
        params$N,
        1/params$T,
        min(comp)
      ) > 0
    ) {
      0
    } else {
      uniroot(
        upperCI,
        c(0.00001, 1),
        N=params$N,
        breaks=1/params$T,
        lb=min(comp)
      )$root
    }
  )
}

anncomp <- function(params, comp, xlim, ylim, cylim) {

  cp <- critP(comp, params)

  nv <- numvess(
    params(
      params$N,
      1/params$T,
      cp
    )
  )

  nvessscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    ylim
  )

  polygon(
    c(cp[2], cp[2], 0, 0, cp[1], cp[1]),
    c(0, nv[2], nv[2], nv[1], nv[1], 0),
    col="gray90",
    border=NA
  )

  text(
    0,
    nv[1],
    paste(
      round(nv[1]),
      " (",
      round(100*nv[1]/params$N),
      "%)",
      sep=""
    ),
    adj=c(0, 0),
    col="gray"
  )

  text(
    0,
    nv[2],
    paste(
      round(nv[2]),
      " (",
      round(100*nv[2]/params$N),
      "%)",
      sep=""
    ),
    adj=c(0, 1),
    col="gray"
  )

  compscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    cylim
  )

  segments(
    1,
    min(comp),
    cp[2],
    comp,
    col="gray"
  )

  segments(
    1,
    max(comp),
    cp[1],
    comp,
    col="gray"
  )

  text(
    1,
    comp,
    paste(comp, collapse="-"),
    adj=c(1, 0),
    col="gray"
  )
}

plotPars <- function(params, comp, xlim=NULL, ylim=NULL) {

  mean <- expmeancomp(params)

  var <- 2*sqrt(
    varmeancomp(params)
  )

  lb <- mean - var
  ub <- mean + var

  par(
    mar=c(5, 4, 4, 4)
  )

  if (is.null(ylim)) {

    cylim <- ylim

  } else {

    cylim <- c(
      1 +
        ((ylim[1] - 1) /
           (params$N - 1)) *
        (params$T - 1),

      1 +
        ((ylim[2] - 1) /
           (params$N - 1)) *
        (params$T - 1)
    )
  }

  nvessscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    ylim,
    new=FALSE
  )

  compscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    cylim
  )

  polygon(
    c(params$p, rev(params$p)),
    c(lb, rev(ub)),
    col="gray90",
    border=NA
  )

  anncomp(
    params,
    comp,
    xlim,
    ylim,
    cylim
  )

  nvessscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    ylim
  )

  mtext(
    "Number of Vessels",
    side=2,
    line=3
  )

  mtext(
    "Sampling Fraction",
    side=1,
    line=3
  )

  lines(
    params$p,
    numvess(params)
  )

  par(new=TRUE)

  compscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    cylim
  )

  mtext(
    "Completeness",
    side=4,
    line=3
  )

  axis(4)

  lines(
    params$p,
    mean,
    lty="dashed"
  )

  lines(
    params$p,
    lb,
    lty="dotted"
  )

  lines(
    params$p,
    ub,
    lty="dotted"
  )

  mtext(
    paste(
      "N = ",
      round(params$N),
      "     brokenness = ",
      round(1/params$T, 3),
      sep=""
    ),
    side=3,
    line=2
  )
}

par(
  cex=0.8,
  mar=c(3, 3, 3, 3)
)

p6 <- params(
  estN(1.2, 0.5, 200),
  0.5
)

plotPars(
  p6,
  1.2
)

nvessscale(
  p6,
  NULL,
  NULL
)

pcrit <- 1 -
  (
    1 -
      200 /
      estN(1.2, 0.5, 200)
  )^(1/p6$T)

lines(
  c(0, pcrit),
  c(200, 200)
)

lines(
  c(pcrit, pcrit),
  c(200, 0)
)








What I noticed. A lot of this code looks busy, but most of the early part is really just math and helper functions, so the plot window does not change yet. The drawing starts once plotPars() gets involved. nvessscale(..., new=FALSE) sets up the first plot, compscale() gives it the second scale, polygon() adds the gray band, and anncomp() adds the shaded area plus the extra lines and text. Then the mtext(), axis(), and lines() calls keep building on that same figure. The comment saying plotPars() is the part to watch makes sense after running it line by line because that is where most of the visible action happens.




# Produce a plot of tiger populations with picture as background
# Source: http://www.globaltiger.org/population.html

year <- c(1993, 1996, 1998, 2001)
minpop <- c(20, 50, 50, 115)
maxpop <- c(50, 240, 240, 150)

library(grid)
library(grImport)
require(colorspace)

# Get the original tiger.ps.xml and grayify.R files
# from the older RGraphics package
old_pkg <- tempfile(fileext = ".tar.gz")
old_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "RGraphics_old")

dir.create(old_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

download.file(
  "https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/RGraphics/RGraphics_2.0-14.tar.gz",
  old_pkg,
  mode = "wb"
)

untar(
  old_pkg,
  files = c(
    "RGraphics/inst/extra/tiger.ps.xml",
    "RGraphics/inst/extra/grayify.R"
  ),
  exdir = old_dir
)

tiger_file <- file.path(
  old_dir,
  "RGraphics",
  "inst",
  "extra",
  "tiger.ps.xml"
)

grayify_file <- file.path(
  old_dir,
  "RGraphics",
  "inst",
  "extra",
  "grayify.R"
)

tiger <- grImport::readPicture(tiger_file)[-1]

source(grayify_file)

grid.newpage()

pushViewport(plotViewport(c(3, 2, 2, 1)),
             viewport(xscale=c(1991, 2003), yscale=c(0, 250)))

grid.rect()

# tiger backdrop in gray
grImport::grid.picture(tiger, x=0.45, FUN=grayify, min=.8)

grid.xaxis(at=year, gp=gpar(cex=0.7))
grid.yaxis(gp=gpar(cex=0.7))

# black bars
grid.rect(x=unit(year, "native"), y=0,
          width=unit(1, "native"), height=unit(maxpop, "native"),
          just="bottom", gp=gpar(fill="black"))

# tiger in bars
tigerGrob <- grImport::pictureGrob(tiger, x=0.45,
                                   FUN=grImport::grobify)

# Start from 2 because bar 1 does not overlap with tiger
for (i in 2:length(year)) {
    grid.clip(x=unit(year[i], "native"), y=0,
              width=unit(1, "native"),
              height=unit(maxpop[i], "native"),
              just="bottom")

    # tiger backdrop (shift slightly to left so get one eye in one bar)
    grid.draw(tigerGrob)
}

grid.clip()

# redo bar borders
grid.rect(x=unit(year, "native"), y=0,
          width=unit(1, "native"), height=unit(maxpop, "native"),
          just="bottom", gp=gpar(fill=NA))

grid.text("Estimated Population (max.) of Bengal Tigers\n(in Bhutan)",
          y=unit(1, "npc") + unit(1, "lines"))

popViewport(2)








What I noticed. The first part is mostly setup. The population values are created, the old tiger files are pulled in, and the picture object gets prepared. Nothing really appears until grid.newpage() and the viewport are set up. From there, grid.rect() gives the plot its frame, grid.picture() puts the gray tiger in the background, and the axis calls add the years and population scale. The black bars come next, and then the loop clips the tiger image to each bar so parts of the tiger show inside them. The last rectangle call redraws the bar outlines and grid.text() puts the title on top. I had to use Murrell’s already-converted tiger files from the archived RGraphics package because the old PostScript tracing step was not working with the current Ghostscript setup, but the actual drawing idea stays the same.

#
# Comment:
#
# Inspired by Figure 3.3 from
# Wickham's book "ggplot2"
#

library(ggplot2)

print(
  ggplot(
    data = ggplot2::mpg,
    aes(
      x = displ,

    )
  ) +
    geom_point() +

      method = "lm",

What I noticed. This worked a little differently from the base R examples because the pieces build a ggplot object first. ggplot() sets the data and mappings, then geom_point(), stat_smooth(), scale_shape_manual(), and theme_bw() keep adding pieces to that object. The finished graph does not actually hit the graphics device until the outer print(...) runs.




#
# Comment:
#
# A bit of mucking around is required to get the second (whole-world)
# map positioned correctly; this provides an example of calling a
# plotting function to perform calculations but do no drawing (see the
# second call to the map() function).
#
# Makes use of the "maps", "mapdata", and "mapproj" packages to draw the maps.
#

library(maps)
library(mapdata)
library(mapproj)

par(mar=rep(1, 4))

maps::map("nzHires", fill=TRUE, col="gray80",
          regions=c("North Island", "South Island", "Stewart Island"))

points(174.75, -36.87, pch=16, cex=2,
       col=rgb(0,0,0,.5))

arrows(172, -36.87, 174, -36.87, lwd=3)

text(172, -36.87, "Auckland  ",
     adj=1, cex=2, xpd=NA)

# mini world map as guide
maplocs <- maps::map(
  projection="sp_mercator",
  wrap=TRUE,
  lwd=0.1,
  col="gray",
  ylim=c(-60, 75),
  interior=FALSE,
  orientation=c(90, 180, 0),
  add=TRUE,
  plot=FALSE
)

xrange <- range(maplocs$x, na.rm=TRUE)
yrange <- range(maplocs$y, na.rm=TRUE)
aspect <- abs(diff(yrange))/abs(diff(xrange))

# customised to 6.5 by 4.5 figure size
par(
  fig=c(0.99 - 0.5,
        0.99,
        0.01,
        0.01 + 0.5*aspect*4.5/6.5),
  mar=rep(0, 4),
  new=TRUE
)

plot.new()

plot.window(
  xlim=xrange,
  ylim=yrange
)

maps::map(
  projection="sp_mercator",
  wrap=TRUE,
  lwd=0.5,
  ylim=c(-60, 75),
  interior=FALSE,
  orientation=c(90, 180, 0),
  add=TRUE
)

symbols(
  -.13,
  -0.8,
  circles=1,
  inches=0.1,
  add=TRUE,
  bg=rgb(0,0,0,.2)
)

box()








What I noticed. The first map() immediately drew New Zealand, and then points(), arrows(), and text() added the Auckland marker, arrow, and label. The interesting part was the next map(..., plot=FALSE) call because, even though it is a plotting function, nothing new showed up. It was only calculating and returning the projected world-map coordinates. After that, par(fig=..., new=TRUE), plot.new(), and plot.window() made room for the inset, and the next map() actually drew the little world map. symbols() marked New Zealand and box() finished the inset border. # Function to draw a non-summary rect-plus-CI
drawNormalCI <- function(LL, OR, UL, size) {

  grid.rect(
    x = unit(OR, "native"),
    width = unit(size, "snpc"),
    height = unit(size, "snpc"),
    gp = gpar(fill = "black")
  )

  # Draw arrow if exceed col range
  if (
    convertX(
      unit(UL, "native"),
      "npc",
      valueOnly = TRUE
    ) > 1
  ) {

    grid.lines(
      x = unit(c(LL, 1), c("native", "npc")),
      y = 0.5,
      arrow = arrow(
        length = unit(0.05, "inches")
      )
    )

  } else {

    lineCol <- if (
      (
        convertX(
          unit(OR, "native") + unit(0.5 * size, "lines"),
          "native",
          valueOnly = TRUE
        ) > UL
      ) &&
      (
        convertX(
          unit(OR, "native") - unit(0.5 * size, "lines"),
          "native",
          valueOnly = TRUE
        ) < LL
      )
    ) {
      "white"
    } else {
      "black"
    }

    grid.lines(
      x = unit(c(LL, UL), "native"),
      y = 0.5,
      gp = gpar(col = lineCol)
    )
  }
}

# Function to draw a summary "diamond"
drawSummaryCI <- function(LL, OR, UL, size) {

  grid.polygon(
    x = unit(
      c(LL, OR, UL, OR),
      "native"
    ),
    y = unit(
      0.5 + c(
        0,
        0.25 * size,
        0,
        -0.25 * size
      ),
      "npc"
    )
  )
}

# Function to draw a "data" column
drawDataCol <- function(col, j) {

  pushViewport(
    viewport(
      layout.pos.col = j,
      xscale = col$range
    )
  )

  grid.lines(
    x = unit(1, "native"),
    y = 0:1
  )

  # Assume that last value in col is "All"
  grid.lines(
    x = unit(
      col$OR[length(col$OR)],
      "native"
    ),
    y = 0:1,
    gp = gpar(lty = "dashed")
  )

  grid.xaxis(
    gp = gpar(cex = 0.6)
  )

  grid.text(
    "OR",
    y = unit(-2, "lines")
  )

  popViewport()

  for (i in 1:length(col$rows)) {

    pushViewport(
      viewport(
        layout.pos.row = col$rows[i],
        layout.pos.col = j,
        xscale = col$range
      )
    )

    if (col$type[i] == "n") {
      drawNormalCI(
        col$LL[i],
        col$OR[i],
        col$UL[i],
        col$sizes[i]
      )
    } else {
      drawSummaryCI(
        col$LL[i],
        col$OR[i],
        col$UL[i],
        col$sizes[i]
      )
    }

    popViewport()
  }
}

What I noticed. Most of this chunk is basically building all the pieces before anything gets drawn. The lists store the labels and numbers, and the helper functions explain how each part should be drawn later. The actual figure comes together near the end, which matches the comment in the code. The big pushViewport() makes the table layout, grid.rect() creates the dark header and gray summary rows, drawLabelCol() fills in the text columns, and drawDataCol() handles the odds-ratio side with the confidence intervals, boxes, arrows, and diamonds. Inside those helper functions, the grid.* calls are the ones actually changing what I see.

What I noticed. There is a lot of coordinate math in this one, but most of that math does not change the device at all. par(mfrow=c(2,1), ...) first splits the page into two panels, and each plot(..., type="n") gives the next panel an empty coordinate system. From there the outer circles, gray areas, latitude and longitude curves, planes, and thick axes are added little by little with lines() and polygon(). The loops are basically repeating those drawing calls for a bunch of calculated coordinates. The text() calls label the X1, X2, and X3 axes. This one made a lot more sense once I separated the coordinate calculations from the lines that actually draw.




library(grid)
library(colorspace)

uoaBlue <- "#00467f"

uoaLCH <- colorspace::coords(
  as(colorspace::hex2RGB(uoaBlue), "polarLUV")
)

hues <- c(
  uoaLCH[3],
  uoaLCH[3] + 90,
  uoaLCH[3] + 180,
  uoaLCH[3] + 270
)

darks <- hcl(
  hues,
  uoaLCH[2],
  uoaLCH[1]
)

lights <- hcl(
  hues,
  uoaLCH[2],
  80
)

arr <- arrow(
  length = unit(2, "mm"),
  type = "closed"

document <- function(
  label,
  x = .5,
  y = .5,
  w = unit(2, "cm"),
  h = unit(3, "cm"),
  d = unit(6, "mm"),
  ann = TRUE,
  border = NA,
  fill = NULL,
  name = "script"
) {

  if (is.null(fill)) {
    fill <- lights[1]
  }

  pushViewport(
    viewport(
      x,
      y,
      w,
      h,
      name = "scriptvp"
    )
  )

  grid.polygon(
    unit.c(
      unit(0, "npc"),
      unit(0, "npc"),
      unit(1, "npc"),
      unit(1, "npc"),
      d,
      d,
      unit(0, "npc")
    ),
    unit.c(
      unit(1, "npc") - d,
      unit(0, "npc"),
      unit(0, "npc"),
      unit(1, "npc"),
      unit(1, "npc"),
      unit(1, "npc") - d,
      unit(1, "npc") - d
    ),
    gp = gpar(
      col = border,
      fill = fill
    ),
    name = name
  )

  grid.polygon(
    unit.c(
      unit(0, "npc"),
      d,
      d
    ),
    unit.c(
      unit(1, "npc") - d,
      unit(1, "npc") - d,
      unit(1, "npc")
    ),
    gp = gpar(
      col = NA,
      fill = darks[1]
    )
  )

  grid.text(label)

  if (ann) {

    grid.rect(
      y = 0,
      height = unit(2, "lines"),
      just = "top",
      gp = gpar(
        col = NA,
        fill = darks[1]
      )
    )

    grid.segments(
      0,
      0,
      1,
      0,
      gp = gpar(
        col = "white",
        lwd = 2
      )
    )

    grid.text(
      "SCRIPT",
      gp = gpar(col = "white"),
      y = unit(-1, "lines")
    )
  }

  upViewport()
}

module <- function(
  label,
  nin,
  nout,
  x = .5,
  y = .5,
  w = unit(3, "cm"),
  h = unit(4, "cm"),
  ann = TRUE,
  border = NA,
  labelin = TRUE,
  labelout = TRUE,
  inoutext = .2,
  arrowsin = TRUE,
  arrowsout = TRUE
) {

  pushViewport(
    viewport(
      x,
      y,
      w,
      h,
      name = "modulevp"
    )
  )

  grid.rect(
    gp = gpar(
      col = border,
      fill = lights[2]
    )
  )

  document(
    label,
    ann = FALSE,
    border = darks[1],
    name = label
  )

  if (arrowsin) {
    arrin <- arr
  } else {
    arrin <- NULL
  }

  if (arrowsout) {
    arrout <- arr
  } else {
    arrout <- NULL
  }

  if (nin > 0) {

    grid.segments(
      -inoutext,
      1:nin/(nin + 1),
      grobX(
        rectGrob(vp = "scriptvp"),
        180
      ),
      1:nin/(nin + 1),
      gp = gpar(
        lwd = 3,
        col = "black"
      ),
      arrow = arrin
    )

    if (is.character(labelin)) {
      lab <- labelin
      fam <- "mono"

    } else if (labelin) {
      lab <- "IN"
      fam <- "sans"

    } else {
      lab <- NULL
    }

    if (!is.null(lab)) {

      grid.text(
        lab,
        unit(-inoutext, "npc") - unit(2, "mm"),
        1:nin/(nin + 1),
        just = "right",
        gp = gpar(
          cex = .7,
          fontfamily = fam
        )
      )
    }
  }

  if (nout > 0) {

    grid.segments(
      grobX(
        rectGrob(vp = "scriptvp"),
        0
      ),
      1:nout/(nout + 1),
      1 + inoutext,
      1:nout/(nout + 1),
      gp = gpar(
        lwd = 3,
        col = "black"
      ),
      arrow = arrout
    )

    if (is.character(labelout)) {
      lab <- labelout
      fam <- "mono"

    } else if (labelout) {
      lab <- "OUT"
      fam <- "sans"

    } else {
      lab <- NULL
    }

    if (!is.null(lab)) {

      grid.text(
        lab,
        unit(1 + inoutext, "npc") + unit(2, "mm"),
        1:nout/(nout + 1),
        just = "left",
        gp = gpar(
          cex = .7,
          fontfamily = fam
        )
      )
    }
  }

  if (ann) {

    grid.rect(
      y = 0,
      height = unit(2, "lines"),
      just = "top",
      gp = gpar(
        col = NA,
        fill = darks[2]
      )
    )

    grid.segments(
      0,
      0,
      1,
      0,
      gp = gpar(
        col = "white",
        lwd = 2
      )
    )

    grid.text(
      "MODULE",
      gp = gpar(col = "white"),
      y = unit(0, "npc") - unit(1, "lines")
    )
  }

  upViewport()
}

pipeline <- function(
  x = .5,

) {

  pushViewport(

    )
  )

  grid.rect(
    gp = gpar(

    )

  if (modules) {

    module(
      "R",
      1,
      2,
      x = 1/4,
      labelout = FALSE,
      inoutext = .5,
      arrowsout = FALSE,
      ann = FALSE,
      border = darks[2]

      "Python",
      2,
      1,
      x = 3/4,
      labelin = FALSE,
      inoutext = .5,
      ann = FALSE,
      border = darks[2]
    )
  }

  grid.rect(
    y = 0,
    height = unit(2, "lines"),
    just = "top",
    gp = gpar(
      col = NA,
      fill = darks[4]
    )
  )

  grid.segments(
    0,
    0,
    1,
    0,
    gp = gpar(
      col = "white",
      lwd = 2
    )
  )

  grid.text(
    "PIPELINE",
    gp = gpar(col = "white"),
    y = unit(0, "npc") - unit(1, "lines")
  )

  upViewport()
}

Then grid.polygon() puts the transparent red section over it. The rectangle and text-grob calls build the two white label boxes, the dotted segments point them toward the graphic, and the last viewport creates the black headline area at the top. I also use the archived RGraphics copy of AfterTheBombs.jpg if the installed package does not have it. That only changes how the image file is found, not how the figure itself is drawn.




library(grid)

size <- unit(.5, "in")

node <- function(text, x, y, fill = "grey") {
  grid.circle(
    x, y,
    r = size,
    gp = gpar(fill = fill),
    name = text
  )
  grid.text(text, x, y)
}

edge <- function(from, fangle, to, tangle, ends = "last") {
  grid.segments(
    grobX(from, fangle), grobY(from, fangle),
    grobX(to, tangle), grobY(to, tangle),
    arrow = arrow(angle = 15, type = "closed", ends = ends),
    gp = gpar(fill = "black")
  )
}

curve <- function(from, fangle, to, tangle, curv, ends = "last") {
  x1 <- convertX(grobX(from, fangle), "in")
  y1 <- convertY(grobY(from, fangle), "in")
  x2 <- convertX(grobX(to, tangle), "in")
  y2 <- convertY(grobY(to, tangle), "in")

  grid.curve(
    x1, y1, x2, y2,
    curvature = curv,
    ncp = 5,
    square = FALSE,
    arrow = arrow(angle = 15, type = "closed", ends = ends),
    gp = gpar(fill = "black")
  )
}

What I noticed. The first few lines just decide the node size and define the helper functions, so the page stays blank. grid.newpage() starts the actual figure. Every node() call then adds one circle with its label, every edge() call adds a straight arrow between two packages, and the calls with ends="both" put arrows on both ends. The final curve() call is the only curved connection, linking graphics to gridGraphics.

# Persp

y <- x

  10 * sin(r) / r
}

z <- outer(x, y, f)
z[is.na(z)] <- 1

# 0.5 to include z axis label

  theta=30,
  phi=30,
  expand=0.5

# Piechart
# Example 4 from help(pie)

par(mar=c(0, 2, 1, 2), xpd=FALSE, cex=0.5)

pie.sales <- c(
  0.12,
  0.3,
  0.26,

  0.04,

)

  "Blueberry",
  "Cherry",
  "Apple",
  "Boston Cream",
  "Other",
  "Vanilla"
)

  col=gray(seq(0.3, 1.0, length=6))

What I noticed. This one made the difference between setting up a plot and actually drawing on it pretty obvious. par(mfrow=c(3,2)) split the device into six spots. For the scatterplot, plot.new() gave me a blank frame and plot.window() set the coordinates, but the actual graph started filling in when the lines() and points() calls ran. The three axis() calls added the bottom, left, and right axes, then box(), mtext(), and text() filled in the border and labels. The same idea showed up in the other panels: hist(), barplot(), boxplot(), persp(), and pie() made the main plots, while functions like lines(), mtext(), text(), and legend() added extra pieces. The assignments and calculations did not visibly change the device. Also, names() only gave the pie values their category names; it did not draw anything.

title: Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
text:
#
# Comment:
#
# A sophisticated example of adding further output to a basic plot.
#
# Most of the functions defined are just for calculating values
# relevant to the data analysis.
#
# The function plotPars() is the one of interest for seeing how
# the drawing of the plot is done.
#

params <- function(N, breaks, p=seq(0.001, 1, length=100)) {
  list(
    N=N,
    T=1/breaks,
    p=p,
    q=1-p
  )
}

pdfcomp <- function(comp, params) {
  n <- params$T
  p <- params$p
  q <- params$q
  y <- round(comp/n)

  choose(n, comp) * p^comp * q^(n-comp) / (1 - q^n)
}

# Expected num sherds (for a vessel) [=completeness]
expcomp <- function(params) {
  params$T * params$p / (1 - params$q^params$T)
}

# Variance of num sherds (for a vessel)
varcomp <- function(params) {
  n <- params$T
  p <- params$p
  q <- params$q

  # From Johnson & Kotz
  (n*p*q / (1 - q^n)) -
    (n^2*p^2*q^n / (1 - q^n)^2)

  # n^2 times Thomas Yee's formula
  # n^2*((p*(1 + p*(n - 1)) / (n*(1 - q^n))) -
  #       (p^2 / (1 - q^n)^2))
}

# Expected value of completeness (for a sample of vessels)
expmeancomp <- function(params) {
  expcomp(params)
}

# Variance of completeness (for a sample of vessels)
# Use the expected number of vessels in sample as denominator
varmeancomp <- function(params) {
  varcomp(params) / numvess(params)
}

numvess <- function(params) {
  params$N * (1 - params$q^params$T)
}

ecomp <- function(p, T, comp) {
  q <- 1 - p
  T*p / (1 - q^T) - comp
}

estN <- function(comp, broke, n) {
  T <- 1/broke

  n / (
    1 -
      (
        1 -
          uniroot(
            ecomp,
            c(0.00001, 1),
            T=T,
            comp=comp
          )$root
      )^T
  )
}

nvessscale <- function(params, xlim, ylim, new=TRUE) {

  if (new)
    par(new=TRUE)

  plot(
    0:1,
    c(1, params$N),
    type="n",
    axes=!new,
    ann=FALSE,
    xlim=xlim,
    ylim=ylim
  )
}

compscale <- function(params, xlim, ylim, new=TRUE) {

  if (new)
    par(new=TRUE)

  plot(
    0:1,
    c(1, params$T),
    type="n",
    axes=!new,
    ann=FALSE,
    xlim=xlim,
    ylim=ylim
  )
}

lowerCI <- function(p, N, breaks, lb) {

  params <- params(N, breaks, p)

  expmeancomp(params) -
    2*sqrt(varmeancomp(params)) -
    lb
}

upperCI <- function(p, N, breaks, lb) {

  params <- params(N, breaks, p)

  expmeancomp(params) +
    2*sqrt(varmeancomp(params)) -
    lb
}

critP <- function(comp, params) {

  c(
    uniroot(
      lowerCI,
      c(0.00001, 1),
      N=params$N,
      breaks=1/params$T,
      lb=max(comp)
    )$root,

    if (
      upperCI(
        0.00001,
        params$N,
        1/params$T,
        min(comp)
      ) > 0
    ) {
      0
    } else {
      uniroot(
        upperCI,
        c(0.00001, 1),
        N=params$N,
        breaks=1/params$T,
        lb=min(comp)
      )$root
    }
  )
}

anncomp <- function(params, comp, xlim, ylim, cylim) {

  cp <- critP(comp, params)

  nv <- numvess(
    params(
      params$N,
      1/params$T,
      cp
    )
  )

  nvessscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    ylim
  )

  polygon(
    c(cp[2], cp[2], 0, 0, cp[1], cp[1]),
    c(0, nv[2], nv[2], nv[1], nv[1], 0),
    col="gray90",
    border=NA
  )

  text(
    0,
    nv[1],
    paste(
      round(nv[1]),
      " (",
      round(100*nv[1]/params$N),
      "%)",
      sep=""
    ),
    adj=c(0, 0),
    col="gray"
  )

  text(
    0,
    nv[2],
    paste(
      round(nv[2]),
      " (",
      round(100*nv[2]/params$N),
      "%)",
      sep=""
    ),
    adj=c(0, 1),
    col="gray"
  )

  compscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    cylim
  )

  segments(
    1,
    min(comp),
    cp[2],
    comp,
    col="gray"
  )

  segments(
    1,
    max(comp),
    cp[1],
    comp,
    col="gray"
  )

  text(
    1,
    comp,
    paste(comp, collapse="-"),
    adj=c(1, 0),
    col="gray"
  )
}

plotPars <- function(params, comp, xlim=NULL, ylim=NULL) {

  mean <- expmeancomp(params)

  var <- 2*sqrt(
    varmeancomp(params)
  )

  lb <- mean - var
  ub <- mean + var

  par(
    mar=c(5, 4, 4, 4)
  )

  if (is.null(ylim)) {

    cylim <- ylim

  } else {

    cylim <- c(
      1 +
        ((ylim[1] - 1) /
           (params$N - 1)) *
        (params$T - 1),

      1 +
        ((ylim[2] - 1) /
           (params$N - 1)) *
        (params$T - 1)
    )
  }

  nvessscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    ylim,
    new=FALSE
  )

  compscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    cylim
  )

  polygon(
    c(params$p, rev(params$p)),
    c(lb, rev(ub)),
    col="gray90",
    border=NA
  )

  anncomp(
    params,
    comp,
    xlim,
    ylim,
    cylim
  )

  nvessscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    ylim
  )

  mtext(
    "Number of Vessels",
    side=2,
    line=3
  )

  mtext(
    "Sampling Fraction",
    side=1,
    line=3
  )

  lines(
    params$p,
    numvess(params)
  )

  par(new=TRUE)

  compscale(
    params,
    xlim,
    cylim
  )

  mtext(
    "Completeness",
    side=4,
    line=3
  )

  axis(4)

  lines(
    params$p,
    mean,
    lty="dashed"
  )

  lines(
    params$p,
    lb,
    lty="dotted"
  )

  lines(
    params$p,
    ub,
    lty="dotted"
  )

  mtext(
    paste(
      "N = ",
      round(params$N),
      "     brokenness = ",
      round(1/params$T, 3),
      sep=""
    ),
    side=3,
    line=2
  )
}

par(
  cex=0.8,
  mar=c(3, 3, 3, 3)
)

p6 <- params(
  estN(1.2, 0.5, 200),
  0.5
)

plotPars(
  p6,
  1.2
)

nvessscale(
  p6,
  NULL,
  NULL
)

pcrit <- 1 -
  (
    1 -
      200 /
      estN(1.2, 0.5, 200)
  )^(1/p6$T)

lines(
  c(0, pcrit),
  c(200, 200)
)

lines(
  c(pcrit, pcrit),
  c(200, 0)
)








What I noticed. A lot of this code looks busy, but most of the early part is really just math and helper functions, so the plot window does not change yet. The drawing starts once plotPars() gets involved. nvessscale(..., new=FALSE) sets up the first plot, compscale() gives it the second scale, polygon() adds the gray band, and anncomp() adds the shaded area plus the extra lines and text. Then the mtext(), axis(), and lines() calls keep building on that same figure. The comment saying plotPars() is the part to watch makes sense after running it line by line because that is where most of the visible action happens.

title: Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
text:
# Produce a plot of tiger populations with picture as background
# Source: http://www.globaltiger.org/population.html

year <- c(1993, 1996, 1998, 2001)
minpop <- c(20, 50, 50, 115)
maxpop <- c(50, 240, 240, 150)

library(grid)
library(grImport)
require(colorspace)

# Get the original tiger.ps.xml and grayify.R files
# from the older RGraphics package
old_pkg <- tempfile(fileext = ".tar.gz")
old_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "RGraphics_old")

dir.create(old_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

download.file(
  "https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/RGraphics/RGraphics_2.0-14.tar.gz",
  old_pkg,
  mode = "wb"
)

untar(
  old_pkg,
  files = c(
    "RGraphics/inst/extra/tiger.ps.xml",
    "RGraphics/inst/extra/grayify.R"
  ),
  exdir = old_dir
)

tiger_file <- file.path(
  old_dir,
  "RGraphics",
  "inst",
  "extra",
  "tiger.ps.xml"
)

grayify_file <- file.path(
  old_dir,
  "RGraphics",
  "inst",
  "extra",
  "grayify.R"
)

tiger <- grImport::readPicture(tiger_file)[-1]

source(grayify_file)

grid.newpage()

pushViewport(plotViewport(c(3, 2, 2, 1)),
             viewport(xscale=c(1991, 2003), yscale=c(0, 250)))

grid.rect()

# tiger backdrop in gray
grImport::grid.picture(tiger, x=0.45, FUN=grayify, min=.8)

grid.xaxis(at=year, gp=gpar(cex=0.7))
grid.yaxis(gp=gpar(cex=0.7))

# black bars
grid.rect(x=unit(year, "native"), y=0,
          width=unit(1, "native"), height=unit(maxpop, "native"),
          just="bottom", gp=gpar(fill="black"))

# tiger in bars
tigerGrob <- grImport::pictureGrob(tiger, x=0.45,
                                   FUN=grImport::grobify)

# Start from 2 because bar 1 does not overlap with tiger
for (i in 2:length(year)) {
    grid.clip(x=unit(year[i], "native"), y=0,
              width=unit(1, "native"),
              height=unit(maxpop[i], "native"),
              just="bottom")

    # tiger backdrop (shift slightly to left so get one eye in one bar)
    grid.draw(tigerGrob)
}

grid.clip()

# redo bar borders
grid.rect(x=unit(year, "native"), y=0,
          width=unit(1, "native"), height=unit(maxpop, "native"),
          just="bottom", gp=gpar(fill=NA))

grid.text("Estimated Population (max.) of Bengal Tigers\n(in Bhutan)",
          y=unit(1, "npc") + unit(1, "lines"))

popViewport(2)








What I noticed. The first part is mostly setup. The population values are created, the old tiger files are pulled in, and the picture object gets prepared. Nothing really appears until grid.newpage() and the viewport are set up. From there, grid.rect() gives the plot its frame, grid.picture() puts the gray tiger in the background, and the axis calls add the years and population scale. The black bars come next, and then the loop clips the tiger image to each bar so parts of the tiger show inside them. The last rectangle call redraws the bar outlines and grid.text() puts the title on top. I had to use Murrell’s already-converted tiger files from the archived RGraphics package because the old PostScript tracing step was not working with the current Ghostscript setup, but the actual drawing idea stays the same.

text:
#
# Comment:
#
# A bit of mucking around is required to get the second (whole-world)
# map positioned correctly; this provides an example of calling a
# plotting function to perform calculations but do no drawing (see the
# second call to the map() function).
#
# Makes use of the "maps", "mapdata", and "mapproj" packages to draw the maps.
#

library(maps)
library(mapdata)
library(mapproj)

par(mar=rep(1, 4))

maps::map("nzHires", fill=TRUE, col="gray80",
          regions=c("North Island", "South Island", "Stewart Island"))

points(174.75, -36.87, pch=16, cex=2,
       col=rgb(0,0,0,.5))

arrows(172, -36.87, 174, -36.87, lwd=3)

text(172, -36.87, "Auckland  ",
     adj=1, cex=2, xpd=NA)

# mini world map as guide
maplocs <- maps::map(
  projection="sp_mercator",
  wrap=TRUE,
  lwd=0.1,
  col="gray",
  ylim=c(-60, 75),
  interior=FALSE,
  orientation=c(90, 180, 0),
  add=TRUE,
  plot=FALSE
)

xrange <- range(maplocs$x, na.rm=TRUE)
yrange <- range(maplocs$y, na.rm=TRUE)
aspect <- abs(diff(yrange))/abs(diff(xrange))

# customised to 6.5 by 4.5 figure size
par(
  fig=c(0.99 - 0.5,
        0.99,
        0.01,
        0.01 + 0.5*aspect*4.5/6.5),
  mar=rep(0, 4),
  new=TRUE
)

plot.new()

plot.window(
  xlim=xrange,
  ylim=yrange
)

maps::map(
  projection="sp_mercator",
  wrap=TRUE,
  lwd=0.5,
  ylim=c(-60, 75),
  interior=FALSE,
  orientation=c(90, 180, 0),
  add=TRUE
)

symbols(
  -.13,
  -0.8,
  circles=1,
  inches=0.1,
  add=TRUE,
  bg=rgb(0,0,0,.2)
)

box()








What I noticed. The first map() immediately drew New Zealand, and then points(), arrows(), and text() added the Auckland marker, arrow, and label. The interesting part was the next map(..., plot=FALSE) call because, even though it is a plotting function, nothing new showed up. It was only calculating and returning the projected world-map coordinates. After that, par(fig=..., new=TRUE), plot.new(), and plot.window() made room for the inset, and the next map() actually drew the little world map. symbols() marked New Zealand and box() finished the inset border. So that original comment is basically pointing out that a plotting function can still be used just for calculations.

library(grid)

library(ipred)

# CLASSIFICATION
# fitting
data("GlaucomaM", package = "TH.data")

glau <- GlaucomaM

levels(glau$Class) <- c("glau", "norm")

fm.class <- party::ctree(
  Class ~ .,
  data = glau
)

# visualization
pushViewport(
  viewport(
    gp = gpar(cex = 0.6)
  )
)

plot(
  fm.class,
  newpage = FALSE
)

popViewport()








What I noticed. Everything up through ctree() is really just getting the data and model ready, so the graphics device stays unchanged. pushViewport() sets up the Grid drawing area, and plot(fm.class, newpage=FALSE) is where the tree actually appears. popViewport() just backs out of that drawing area afterward. The published snippet also refers to a custom myNode panel that is not defined in the Chapter 1 snippet, so I used the tree’s regular terminal-node display instead of inventing a missing function.

library(grid)

#
# Comment:
#
# Some simple ideas as a basis for meta-analysis plots.
#
# The code is modular so that something similar could be achieved
# with different data quite simply. The actual drawing for these data
# only occurs in the last 10 or so lines of code.
#

# The horizontal gap between columns with content
colgap <- unit(3, "mm")

# The data for column 1
col1 <- list(
  labels = list(
    textGrob(
      "Centre",
      x = 0,
      just = "left",
      gp = gpar(fontface = "bold", col = "white")
    ),
    textGrob("Thailand", x = 0, just = "left"),
    textGrob("Philippines", x = 0, just = "left"),
    textGrob(
      "All in situ",
      x = 0,
      just = "left",
      gp = gpar(fontface = "bold.italic")
    ),
    textGrob("Colombia", x = 0, just = "left"),
    textGrob("Spain", x = 0, just = "left"),
    textGrob(
      "All invasive",
      x = 0,
      just = "left",
      gp = gpar(fontface = "bold.italic")
    ),
    textGrob(
      "All",
      x = 0,
      just = "left",
      gp = gpar(fontface = "bold")
    )
  ),
  rows = c(1, 5, 6, 8, 11, 12, 14, 16)
)

# Labels in col 1 which are not used to calculate the
# column width (they spill over into col 2)
col1plus <- list(
  labels = list(
    textGrob(
      "Carcinoma in situ",
      x = 0,
      just = "left",
      gp = gpar(fontface = "bold.italic")
    ),
    textGrob(
      "Invasive cancer",
      x = 0,
      just = "left",

# Data for column 2
col2 <- list(
  labels = list(
    textGrob(

      gp = gpar(fontface = "bold", col = "white")
    ),

    ),

    textGrob("115", x = 1, just = "right"),
    textGrob(

    ),
    textGrob(
      "1673",
      x = 1,
      just = "right",
      gp = gpar(fontface = "bold")
    )
  ),
  rows = c(1, 5, 6, 8, 11, 12, 14, 16)
)

# Data for column 3
col3 <- list(
  OR = c(0.72, 1.27, 1.17, 2.97, 1.86, 2.01, 1.20),
  LL = c(0.52, 0.87, 1.03, 1.42, 0.46, 1.09, 1.07),
  UL = c(1.00, 1.85, 1.32, 6.21, 7.51, 3.71, 1.35),
  rows = c(5, 6, 8, 11, 12, 14, 16),
  type = c("n", "n", "s", "n", "n", "s", "s")
)

# Sizes of boxes
information <- sqrt(

)

col3$sizes <- information / max(information)

# Width of column 3
col3width <- unit(1.5, "inches")

# Range on the x-axis for column 3
col3$range <- c(0, 4)

# Function to draw a cell in a text column
drawLabelCol <- function(col, j) {
  for (i in 1:length(col$rows)) {
    pushViewport(
      viewport(
        layout.pos.row = col$rows[i],
        layout.pos.col = j
      )
    )

    grid.draw(col$labels[[i]])

    popViewport()
  }
}

# Function to draw a non-summary rect-plus-CI
drawNormalCI <- function(LL, OR, UL, size) {

  grid.rect(
    x = unit(OR, "native"),
    width = unit(size, "snpc"),
    height = unit(size, "snpc"),
    gp = gpar(fill = "black")
  )

  # Draw arrow if exceed col range
  if (
    convertX(
      unit(UL, "native"),
      "npc",
      valueOnly = TRUE
    ) > 1
  ) {

    grid.lines(
      x = unit(c(LL, 1), c("native", "npc")),
      y = 0.5,
      arrow = arrow(
        length = unit(0.05, "inches")
      )
    )

  } else {

    lineCol <- if (
      (
        convertX(
          unit(OR, "native") + unit(0.5 * size, "lines"),
          "native",
          valueOnly = TRUE
        ) > UL
      ) &&
      (
        convertX(
          unit(OR, "native") - unit(0.5 * size, "lines"),
          "native",
          valueOnly = TRUE
        ) < LL
      )
    ) {
      "white"
    } else {
      "black"
    }

    grid.lines(
      x = unit(c(LL, UL), "native"),
      y = 0.5,
      gp = gpar(col = lineCol)
    )
  }
}

# Function to draw a summary "diamond"
drawSummaryCI <- function(LL, OR, UL, size) {

  grid.polygon(
    x = unit(
      c(LL, OR, UL, OR),
      "native"
    ),
    y = unit(
      0.5 + c(
        0,
        0.25 * size,
        0,
        -0.25 * size
      ),
      "npc"
    )
  )
}

# Function to draw a "data" column
drawDataCol <- function(col, j) {

  pushViewport(
    viewport(
      layout.pos.col = j,
      xscale = col$range
    )
  )

  grid.lines(
    x = unit(1, "native"),
    y = 0:1
  )

  # Assume that last value in col is "All"
  grid.lines(
    x = unit(
      col$OR[length(col$OR)],
      "native"
    ),
    y = 0:1,
    gp = gpar(lty = "dashed")
  )

  grid.xaxis(
    gp = gpar(cex = 0.6)
  )

  grid.text(
    "OR",
    y = unit(-2, "lines")
  )

  popViewport()

  for (i in 1:length(col$rows)) {

    pushViewport(
      viewport(
        layout.pos.row = col$rows[i],
        layout.pos.col = j,
        xscale = col$range
      )
    )

    if (col$type[i] == "n") {
      drawNormalCI(
        col$LL[i],
        col$OR[i],
        col$UL[i],
        col$sizes[i]
      )
    } else {
      drawSummaryCI(
        col$LL[i],
        col$OR[i],
        col$UL[i],
        col$sizes[i]
      )
    }

    popViewport()
  }
}

# Draw the table
pushViewport(
  viewport(
    layout = grid.layout(
      16,
      5,
      widths = unit.c(
        max(
          unit(
            rep(1, 8),
            "grobwidth",
            col1$labels
          )
        ),
        colgap,
        max(
          unit(
            rep(1, 8),
            "grobwidth",
            col2$labels
          )
        ),
        colgap,
        col3width
      ),
      heights = unit(
        c(1, 0, rep(1, 14)),
        "lines"
      )
    )
  )
)

pushViewport(
  viewport(
    layout.pos.row = 1
  )
)

grid.rect(
  gp = gpar(
    col = NA,
    fill = "black"
  )
)

popViewport()

for (i in c(8, 14, 16)) {

  pushViewport(
    viewport(
      layout.pos.row = i
    )
  )

  grid.rect(
    gp = gpar(
      col = NA,
      fill = "gray80"
    )
  )

  popViewport()
}

drawLabelCol(col1, 1)
drawLabelCol(col1plus, 1)
drawLabelCol(col2, 3)
drawDataCol(col3, 5)

popViewport()








What I noticed. Most of this chunk is basically building all the pieces before anything gets drawn. The lists store the labels and numbers, and the helper functions explain how each part should be drawn later. The actual figure comes together near the end, which matches the comment in the code. The big pushViewport() makes the table layout, grid.rect() creates the dark header and gray summary rows, drawLabelCol() fills in the text columns, and drawDataCol() handles the odds-ratio side with the confidence intervals, boxes, arrows, and diamonds. Inside those helper functions, the grid.* calls are the ones actually changing what I see.

xx <- cos(pi/2 - obsphi)*sin(lambdas)

      k1*cos(pi/2 - obsphi)*cos(lambdas)

polygon(xx, yy, col="gray")
lines(xx, yy, lwd=2)

theta1sA <- seq(-obsphi, obsphi, length=500)
theta2sA <- acos(cos(obsphi)/cos(theta1sA))

theta1sB <- seq(obsphi, -obsphi, length=500)
theta2sB <- -acos(cos(obsphi)/cos(theta1sB))

theta2s <- c(theta2sA, theta2sB)

lambda <- pi/4

crit <- acos((-k1*sin(phi))/(k2*cos(phi)))

lambdas <- seq(-crit, crit, length=500)

yy <- k2*sin(phi) -
      k1*cos(phi)*cos(lambdas)

lines(xx, yy, lwd=2)

# Create axes
lines(c(0.00, 0.00),
      c(k2*sin(pi/2), 1.11),
      lwd=4)

lines(c(0.00, 0.00),
      c(-1, -1.12),
      lwd=4)

a2x <- sin(-pi/4)
a2y <- cos(-pi/4)*(-k1)

lines(c(a2x, 1.5*a2x),
      c(a2y, 1.5*a2y),
      lwd=4)

a3x <- sin(pi/4)
a3y <- cos(pi/4)*(-k1)

lines(c(a3x, 1.5*a3x),
      c(a3y, 1.5*a3y),
      lwd=4)

k <- sqrt(a3x^2 + a3y^2)

lines(c(-a3x/k, 1.2*(-a3x/k)),
      c(-a3y/k, 1.2*(-a3y/k)),
      lwd=4)

k <- sqrt(a2x^2 + a2y^2)

lines(c(-a2x/k, 1.2*(-a2x/k)),
      c(-a2y/k, 1.2*(-a2y/k)),
      lwd=4)

# Add text
text(-1.07, -.85, expression(bold(X[2])))
text(1.11, -.85, expression(bold(X[3])))
text(0.1, 1.12, expression(bold(X[1])))

lines(XX, YY, type="l")








What I noticed. There is a lot of coordinate math in this one, but most of that math does not change the device at all. par(mfrow=c(2,1), ...) first splits the page into two panels, and each plot(..., type="n") gives the next panel an empty coordinate system. From there the outer circles, gray areas, latitude and longitude curves, planes, and thick axes are added little by little with lines() and polygon(). The loops are basically repeating those drawing calls for a bunch of calculated coordinates. The text() calls label the X1, X2, and X3 axes. This one made a lot more sense once I separated the coordinate calculations from the lines that actually draw.

library(grid)
library(colorspace)

uoaBlue <- "#00467f"

uoaLCH <- colorspace::coords(
  as(colorspace::hex2RGB(uoaBlue), "polarLUV")
)

hues <- c(
  uoaLCH[3],
  uoaLCH[3] + 90,
  uoaLCH[3] + 180,
  uoaLCH[3] + 270
)

darks <- hcl(
  hues,
  uoaLCH[2],
  uoaLCH[1]
)

lights <- hcl(
  hues,
  uoaLCH[2],
  80
)

arr <- arrow(
  length = unit(2, "mm"),
  type = "closed"
)

document <- function(
  label,
  x = .5,
  y = .5,
  w = unit(2, "cm"),
  h = unit(3, "cm"),
  d = unit(6, "mm"),
  ann = TRUE,
  border = NA,
  fill = NULL,
  name = "script"
) {

  if (is.null(fill)) {
    fill <- lights[1]
  }

  pushViewport(
    viewport(
      x,
      y,
      w,
      h,
      name = "scriptvp"
    )
  )

  grid.polygon(
    unit.c(
      unit(0, "npc"),
      unit(0, "npc"),
      unit(1, "npc"),
      unit(1, "npc"),
      d,
      d,
      unit(0, "npc")
    ),
    unit.c(
      unit(1, "npc") - d,
      unit(0, "npc"),
      unit(0, "npc"),
      unit(1, "npc"),
      unit(1, "npc"),
      unit(1, "npc") - d,
      unit(1, "npc") - d
    ),
    gp = gpar(
      col = border,
      fill = fill
    ),
    name = name
  )

  grid.polygon(
    unit.c(
      unit(0, "npc"),
      d,
      d
    ),
    unit.c(
      unit(1, "npc") - d,
      unit(1, "npc") - d,
      unit(1, "npc")
    ),
    gp = gpar(
      col = NA,
      fill = darks[1]
    )
  )

  grid.text(label)

  if (ann) {

    grid.rect(
      y = 0,
      height = unit(2, "lines"),
      just = "top",
      gp = gpar(
        col = NA,
        fill = darks[1]
      )
    )

    grid.segments(
      0,
      0,
      1,
      0,
      gp = gpar(
        col = "white",
        lwd = 2
      )
    )

    grid.text(
      "SCRIPT",
      gp = gpar(col = "white"),
      y = unit(-1, "lines")
    )
  }

  upViewport()
}

module <- function(
  label,
  nin,
  nout,
  x = .5,
  y = .5,
  w = unit(3, "cm"),
  h = unit(4, "cm"),
  ann = TRUE,
  border = NA,
  labelin = TRUE,
  labelout = TRUE,
  inoutext = .2,
  arrowsin = TRUE,
  arrowsout = TRUE
) {

  pushViewport(
    viewport(
      x,
      y,
      w,
      h,
      name = "modulevp"
    )
  )

  grid.rect(
    gp = gpar(
      col = border,
      fill = lights[2]
    )
  )

  document(
    label,
    ann = FALSE,
    border = darks[1],
    name = label
  )

  if (arrowsin) {
    arrin <- arr
  } else {
    arrin <- NULL
  }

  if (arrowsout) {
    arrout <- arr
  } else {
    arrout <- NULL
  }

  if (nin > 0) {

    grid.segments(
      -inoutext,
      1:nin/(nin + 1),
      grobX(
        rectGrob(vp = "scriptvp"),
        180
      ),
      1:nin/(nin + 1),
      gp = gpar(
        lwd = 3,
        col = "black"
      ),
      arrow = arrin
    )

    if (is.character(labelin)) {
      lab <- labelin
      fam <- "mono"

    } else if (labelin) {
      lab <- "IN"
      fam <- "sans"

    } else {
      lab <- NULL
    }

    if (!is.null(lab)) {

      grid.text(
        lab,
        unit(-inoutext, "npc") - unit(2, "mm"),
        1:nin/(nin + 1),
        just = "right",
        gp = gpar(
          cex = .7,
          fontfamily = fam
        )
      )
    }
  }

  if (nout > 0) {

    grid.segments(
      grobX(
        rectGrob(vp = "scriptvp"),
        0
      ),
      1:nout/(nout + 1),
      1 + inoutext,
      1:nout/(nout + 1),
      gp = gpar(
        lwd = 3,
        col = "black"
      ),
      arrow = arrout
    )

    if (is.character(labelout)) {
      lab <- labelout
      fam <- "mono"

    } else if (labelout) {
      lab <- "OUT"
      fam <- "sans"

    } else {
      lab <- NULL
    }

    if (!is.null(lab)) {

      grid.text(
        lab,
        unit(1 + inoutext, "npc") + unit(2, "mm"),
        1:nout/(nout + 1),
        just = "left",
        gp = gpar(
          cex = .7,
          fontfamily = fam
        )
      )
    }
  }

  if (ann) {

    grid.rect(
      y = 0,
      height = unit(2, "lines"),
      just = "top",
      gp = gpar(
        col = NA,
        fill = darks[2]
      )
    )

    grid.segments(
      0,
      0,
      1,
      0,
      gp = gpar(
        col = "white",
        lwd = 2
      )
    )

    grid.text(
      "MODULE",
      gp = gpar(col = "white"),
      y = unit(0, "npc") - unit(1, "lines")
    )
  }

  upViewport()
}

pipeline <- function(
  x = .5,
  y = .5,
  width = unit(10, "cm"),
  height = unit(6, "cm"),
  modules = TRUE
) {

  pushViewport(
    viewport(
      x,
      y,
      width = width,
      height = height,
      name = "pipelinevp"
    )
  )

  grid.rect(
    gp = gpar(
      col = NA,
      fill = lights[4]
    )
  )

  if (modules) {

    module(
      "R",
      1,
      2,
      x = 1/4,
      labelout = FALSE,
      inoutext = .5,
      arrowsout = FALSE,
      ann = FALSE,
      border = darks[2]
    )

    module(
      "Python",
      2,
      1,
      x = 3/4,
      labelin = FALSE,
      inoutext = .5,
      ann = FALSE,
      border = darks[2]
    )
  }

  grid.rect(
    y = 0,
    height = unit(2, "lines"),
    just = "top",
    gp = gpar(
      col = NA,
      fill = darks[4]
    )
  )

  grid.segments(
    0,
    0,
    1,
    0,
    gp = gpar(
      col = "white",
      lwd = 2
    )
  )

  grid.text(
    "PIPELINE",
    gp = gpar(col = "white"),
    y = unit(0, "npc") - unit(1, "lines")
  )

  upViewport()
}

What I noticed. The color setup and the document(), module(), and pipeline() definitions are just preparation, so nothing shows up from defining them. grid.newpage() starts the blank page, and then calling pipeline() actually draws the large background. After that, the module() calls make the R and Python boxes, document() makes the little folded file icons, and the segment and curve calls connect everything with arrows. downViewport() and upViewport() are useful to notice too because they change where the next thing gets drawn even though they do not draw anything themselves.

library(grid)
library(jpeg)

# Find the original AfterTheBombs.jpg image
pic_file <- system.file(
  "extra",
  "AfterTheBombs.jpg",
  package = "RGraphics"
)

# If the current RGraphics package does not contain the image,
# get the original image from an older RGraphics release
if (pic_file == "" || !file.exists(pic_file)) {

  old_pkg <- tempfile(fileext = ".tar.gz")
  old_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "RGraphics_image")

  dir.create(
    old_dir,
    showWarnings = FALSE,
    recursive = TRUE
  )

  download.file(
    "https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/RGraphics/RGraphics_3.0-1.tar.gz",
    old_pkg,
    mode = "wb"
  )

  untar(
    old_pkg,
    files = "RGraphics/inst/extra/AfterTheBombs.jpg",
    exdir = old_dir
  )

  pic_file <- file.path(
    old_dir,
    "RGraphics",
    "inst",
    "extra",
    "AfterTheBombs.jpg"
  )
}

pic <- jpeg::readJPEG(pic_file)

w <- 1024 # 578
h <- 768 # 500
bg <- pic # [1:h, (1024 - w):1024]

unknown <- 8.7
total <- 9.1
known <- total - unknown

theta0 <- pi/4
thetaN <- theta0 + 2*pi*unknown/total
theta <- seq(theta0, thetaN, length.out=100)

x <- 0.3*c(0, cos(theta)) + 0.5
y <- 0.3*c(0, sin(theta)) + 0.35

grid.newpage()

grid.raster(bg)

  viewport(

    gp=gpar(cex=1.2)
  )
)

grid.polygon(
  x,
  y,
  gp=gpar(
    col=NA,
    fill=rgb(.67, 0, .11, .7)
  )
)

label1 <- textGrob(
  "UNACCOUNTED\nFOR",
  unit(.2, "npc") - unit(2, "mm"),
  unit(.6, "npc") + unit(2, "mm"),
  gp=gpar(
    cex=1.4,
    fontface="bold"
  ),
  just=c("right", "bottom")
)

grid.rect(
  .2,
  .6,
  just=c("right", "bottom"),
  width=grobWidth(label1) + unit(4, "mm"),
  height=grobHeight(label1) + unit(4, "mm"),

  unit(.6, "npc") + unit(2, "mm"),
  gp=gpar(
    cex=1.4,
    fontface="bold"
  ),
  just=c("left", "bottom")
)

grid.rect(
  .8,
  .6,
  just=c("left", "bottom"),
  width=grobWidth(label2) + unit(4, "mm"),
  height=grobHeight(label2) + unit(4, "mm"),
  gp=gpar(
    col=NA,
    fill=rgb(1, 1, 1, .5)
  )
)

grid.draw(label2)

grid.segments(
  c(.2, .8),
  .6,
  c(.3, .7),
  .5,
  gp=gpar(
    lty="dotted",
    lwd=2
  )
)

heading <- textGrob(
  "The Department of Defense is unable to account for the use of
$8.7 billion of the $9.1 billion it spent on reconstruction in Iraq",
  x=unit(0.5, "cm"),
  y=unit(3, "lines"),
  just=c("left", "top"),
  gp=gpar(
    cex=1,
    col="white"
  )
)

pushViewport(
  viewport(
    x=0,
    y=1,
    just=c("left", "top"),
    height=grobHeight(heading) + unit(4, "lines"),
    width=grobWidth(heading) + unit(1, "cm")
  )
)

grid.rect(
  gp=gpar(fill="black")
)

grid.segments(
  x0=unit(0.5, "cm"),
  x1=unit(1, "npc") - unit(0.5, "cm"),
  y0=unit(1, "npc") - unit(2, "lines"),
  y1=unit(1, "npc") - unit(2, "lines"),
  gp=gpar(
    col="grey50",
    lwd=2
  )
)

grid.text(
  "That's 96 Percent",
  x=unit(0.5, "cm"),
  y=unit(1, "npc") - unit(1, "lines"),
  just="left",
  gp=gpar(
    fontface="bold",
    col="white"
  )
)

grid.draw(heading)

popViewport(2)








What I noticed. Reading the JPEG and calculating the red sector happens in the background first, so there is still no figure yet. grid.newpage() starts the page and grid.raster() is when the photo finally appears. Then grid.polygon() puts the transparent red section over it. The rectangle and text-grob calls build the two white label boxes, the dotted segments point them toward the graphic, and the last viewport creates the black headline area at the top. I also use the archived RGraphics copy of AfterTheBombs.jpg if the installed package does not have it. That only changes how the image file is found, not how the figure itself is drawn.

title: Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
