library(grid)

size <- unit(.5, "in")

node <- function(text, x, y, fill = "grey") {
  grid.circle(
    x, y,
    r = size,
    gp = gpar(fill = fill),
    name = text
  )
  grid.text(text, x, y)
}

edge <- function(from, fangle, to, tangle, ends = "last") {
  grid.segments(
    grobX(from, fangle), grobY(from, fangle),
    grobX(to, tangle), grobY(to, tangle),
    arrow = arrow(angle = 15, type = "closed", ends = ends),
    gp = gpar(fill = "black")
  )
}

curve <- function(from, fangle, to, tangle, curv, ends = "last") {
  x1 <- convertX(grobX(from, fangle), "in")
  y1 <- convertY(grobY(from, fangle), "in")
  x2 <- convertX(grobX(to, tangle), "in")
  y2 <- convertY(grobY(to, tangle), "in")

  grid.curve(
    x1, y1, x2, y2,
    curvature = curv,
    ncp = 5,
    square = FALSE,
    arrow = arrow(angle = 15, type = "closed", ends = ends),
    gp = gpar(fill = "black")
  )
}

grid.newpage()

node("grDevices", .5, 3/5)
node("graphics", .5, 4/5)
node("grid", .5, 2/5)
node("lattice", 2/5, 1/5)
node("ggplot2", 3/5, 1/5)
node("grImport", 1/5, 3/5, fill = "white")
node("grImport2", 1/5, 1.5/5, fill = "white")
node("gridBase", 3.5/5, 3/5, fill = "white")
node("gridGraphics", 4.5/5, 2.5/5, fill = "white")
node("gridSVG", 4/5, 1.5/5, fill = "white")

edge("grDevices", 90, "graphics", 270)
edge("grDevices", 270, "grid", 90)
edge("grid", 240, "lattice", 70)
edge("grid", 300, "ggplot2", 110)
edge("grImport2", 20, "grid", 200)
edge("grid", 340, "gridSVG", 160)
edge("grImport", 35, "graphics", 215)
edge("grImport", 325, "grid", 145)
edge("grid", 45, "gridBase", 225, ends = "both")
edge("graphics", 315, "gridBase", 135, ends = "both")
edge("gridGraphics", 190, "grid", 10)
curve("graphics", 20, "gridGraphics", 90, -.5)








What I noticed. The first few lines just decide the node size and define the helper functions, so the page stays blank. grid.newpage() starts the actual figure. Every node() call then adds one circle with its label, every edge() call adds a straight arrow between two packages, and the calls with ends="both" put arrows on both ends. The final curve() call is the only curved connection, linking graphics to gridGraphics.

text:
A. Set Up the Canvas

par()

oldpar <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)

par(
  mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1),
  las = 1,
  cex.axis = 0.8
)

plot(
  hpi2025$life_expectancy,
  hpi2025$hpi,
  pch = 19,
  xlab = "Life expectancy",
  ylab = "Happy Planet Index",
  main = "Life Expectancy and HPI, 2025"
)







par(oldpar)

par() is basically where I control the overall plot setup, like the margins, label direction, text size, or whether I want more than one panel.


box()

plot(
  hpi2025$wellbeing,
  hpi2025$hpi,
  pch = 19,
  bty = "n",
  xlab = "Wellbeing",
  ylab = "Happy Planet Index",
  main = "Wellbeing and HPI, 2025"
)

box(lwd = 2)








box() controls the border around a plot, so I can add the frame after the plotting area is already there.


axis()

plot(
  hpi2025$ecological_footprint,
  hpi2025$hpi,
  pch = 19,
  axes = FALSE,
  xlab = "Ecological footprint",
  ylab = "Happy Planet Index",
  main = "Ecological Footprint and HPI, 2025"
)

axis(
  side = 1,
  at = pretty(hpi2025$ecological_footprint)
)

axis(
  side = 2,

axis() lets me control where an axis goes and what tick marks and labels show up on it.

title: Assignment 2: Base R Graphics
text:
B. Draw Whole Plots

hist()

hist(
  hpi2025$hpi,
  breaks = 12,
  main = "Distribution of Happy Planet Index Scores, 2025",
  xlab = "Happy Planet Index",
  ylab = "Number of countries"
)








hist() makes the full histogram, so it controls how a numeric variable gets grouped into bars and shown as a distribution.


boxplot()

oldpar <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)

par(
  mar = c(8, 4, 3, 1)
)

boxplot(
  hpi ~ group,
  data = hpi2025,
  las = 2,
  xlab = "",
  ylab = "Happy Planet Index",
  main = "Happy Planet Index by Region, 2025"
)







par(oldpar)

boxplot() makes the full box-and-whisker plot, which is useful for comparing the middle, spread, and possible outliers across groups.


pie()

region_table <- table(hpi2025$group)
region_table <- sort(
  region_table,
  decreasing = TRUE
)

pie_values <- as.numeric(region_table)

# names() is part of the workflow, but it is NOT a graphics function.
names(pie_values) <- names(region_table)

pie(
  pie_values,
  main = "Countries in the 2025 HPI Data by Region"
)








pie() makes the whole pie chart, with each slice showing how much of the total comes from each category.


persp()

surface_model <- lm(
  hpi ~ life_expectancy + wellbeing,
  data = hpi2025
)

x_surface <- seq(
  min(hpi2025$life_expectancy),
  max(hpi2025$life_expectancy),
  length.out = 30
)

y_surface <- seq(
  min(hpi2025$wellbeing),
  max(hpi2025$wellbeing),
  length.out = 30
)

b <- coef(surface_model)

z_surface <- outer(
  x_surface,
  y_surface,
  function(x, y) {
    b[1] + b[2] * x + b[3] * y
  }
)

persp(
  x_surface,
  y_surface,
  z_surface,
  theta = 35,
  phi = 25,
  expand = 0.7,
  ticktype = "detailed",
  xlab = "Life expectancy",
  ylab = "Wellbeing",
  zlab = "Predicted HPI",
  main = "Predicted HPI Surface, 2025"
)








persp() controls the 3-D perspective view of a surface made from x, y, and z values.

plot(
  hpi2025$life_expectancy,

Article
Anscombe’s (1973) Graphs in Statistical Analysis showed me that the presentation of results through data visualization facilitates their perception, evaluation, and communication. While the four data sets described in the article have nearly the same mean, variance, correlation, and regression, their graphical presentation reveals significant differences. Therefore, we cannot rely solely on mathematical results when analyzing data since one might miss vital peculiarities. This fact supports the importance of such statistical software packages as R, which allow exploring patterns and relationships between variables visually. By using code, we can construct informative graphics to estimate the connection between two variables, identify influential points, assess the impact of extreme values, and check the data set for nonlinearity. This method is particularly beneficial for constructing and presenting such statistical software products as dashboards visualizing specific insights through graphics. In this product, we might use these considerations to build informative graphics. However, most importantly, Anscombe’s data sets emphasize the importance of not misrepresenting results. By presenting statistical results through graphics, one must remember that they might contain crucial information that might not be revealed in summary statistics.






Figure 8 from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners’ Report on the Cybersecurity Insurance Market, which compares the percentage of claim closure for primary, excess, endorsement cyber insurance policies, as well as the total has certain strengths and weaknesses (NAIC, 2025). The main strength of this chart is its simplicity since the information is presented in the form of a horizontal bar chart and labeled accordingly. Moreover, the value of each bar is indicated on the chart itself, which allows for faster information retrieval. On the other hand, the key limitation of this graph is the lack of comparison since it only shows the percentage of claims closed for different insurance policies. In the chart, the vertical axis starts at 65%, which narrows the scale and hides the difference in the value of each bar. For instance, compared to endorsement policies, which have a 91.52% closure rate, excess policies only have 76.84%, which is significantly less, but the shrinkage of the bars suggests that the difference between the two is only 15%. The figure above also presents “Total” with an 82.05% closing percentage as if it were another category, which might mislead the interpretation of the data. If I were to develop this chart, I would use a scale that starts at 0% and present the total closing percentage as a reference
Citation: National Association of Insurance Commissioners. (2025). Report on the cybersecurity insurance market.

# Define elements in plant art
# Each image corresponds to a different axiom, rules, angle and depth

# Leaf of Fall

axiom="X"
rules=list("X"="F-[[X]+X]+F[+FX]-X", "F"="FF")
angle=22.5
depth=6


for (i in 1:depth) axiom=gsubfn(".", rules, axiom)

actions=str_extract_all(axiom, "\\d*\\+|\\d*\\-|F|L|R|\\[|\\]|\\|") %>% unlist

status=data.frame(x=numeric(0), y=numeric(0), alfa=numeric(0))
points=data.frame(x1 = 0, y1 = 0, x2 = NA, y2 = NA, alfa=90, depth=1)


# Generating data
# Note: may take a minute or two

for (action in actions)
{
  if (action=="F")
  {
    x=points[1, "x1"]+cos(points[1, "alfa"]*(pi/180))
    y=points[1, "y1"]+sin(points[1, "alfa"]*(pi/180))
    points[1,"x2"]=x
    points[1,"y2"]=y
    data.frame(x1 = x, y1 = y, x2 = NA, y2 = NA,
               alfa=points[1, "alfa"],
               depth=points[1,"depth"]) %>% rbind(points)->points
  }
  if (action %in% c("+", "-")){
    alfa=points[1, "alfa"]
    points[1, "alfa"]=eval(parse(text=paste0("alfa",action, angle)))
  }
  if(action=="["){
    data.frame(x=points[1, "x1"], y=points[1, "y1"], alfa=points[1, "alfa"]) %>%
      rbind(status) -> status
    points[1, "depth"]=points[1, "depth"]+1
  }

  if(action=="]"){
    depth=points[1, "depth"]
    points[-1,]->points
    data.frame(x1=status[1, "x"], y1=status[1, "y"], x2=NA, y2=NA,
               alfa=status[1, "alfa"],
               depth=depth-1) %>%
      rbind(points) -> points
    status[-1,]->status
  }
}

This code downloads the TEDS2016 file in Stata format and loads it into R.

library(haven)
library(ggplot2)

TEDS_2016 <- haven::read_dta("https://github.com/datageneration/home/blob/master/DataProgramming/data/TEDS_2016.dta?raw=true")

title: Assignment 1 – Brush up R and Quarto
text: I noticed that some variables are stored as coded numbers instead of clear words, which makes them harder to interpret until labels are added. I also found missing values in multiple columns, which can change results if they are not handled. Finally, some answers are non substantive, such as no response.

title: Assignment 1 – Brush up R and Quarto
text:
Missing values can be handled by removing rows that have missing values for the variables being analyzed or by replacing missing numeric values with a reasonable value such as the mean. For this assignment, I remove rows where Tondu is missing because Tondu is required for the next steps. I also replace missing age values with the average age so age can still be used.

title: Assignment 1 – Brush up R and Quarto
text:
To explore Tondu with categorical variables such as female, DPP, Taiwanese, and Econ_worse, I use cross tabulations and proportions to compare group patterns. To explore Tondu with numeric or ordered variables such as age, income, and education, I compare averages by Tondu category. These methods provide a clear first look at differences across groups.





ggplot(TEDS_clean, aes(x = Tondu)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "deeppink") +
  facet_wrap(~ female)












ggplot(TEDS_clean, aes(x = Tondu)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "deeppink") +
  facet_grid(female ~ DPP)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Q2. Missing data assessment
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

TEDS_2016 %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to = "variable", 
               values_to = "n_missing") %>%
  filter(n_missing > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_missing))

# Visualize missingness
TEDS_2016 %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to = "variable", 
               values_to = "n_missing") %>%
  filter(n_missing > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(variable, n_missing), y = n_missing)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Missing Values by Variable",
       x = NULL, y = "Count of Missing Values") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18)







# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Q3. Variable recoding
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

teds <- TEDS_2016 %>%
  mutate(
    vote = factor(votetsai, 
                  levels = c(0, 1), 
                  labels = c("Other", "Tsai")),
    gender = factor(female, 
                    levels = c(0, 1), 
                    labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    Tondu = as.factor(Tondu),
    Party = as.factor(Party)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(vote, gender, age, edu, income, 
         Taiwanese, Econ_worse, Tondu, Party, DPP) %>%
  drop_na()

       x = "Vote Choice", y = "Age") +

  theme(legend.position = "none")







# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Q8. Correlation matrix
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

teds %>%
  dplyr::select(age, edu, income, Taiwanese, Econ_worse, DPP) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs") %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "cor") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = cor)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(cor, 2)), size = 6) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#e74c3c", mid = "white", high = "#2980b9",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation Matrix of Numeric Variables",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

title: Assignment 3: ML Exercise
text:
Multiple Regression Exercise
This assignment applies ideas from ISLR Chapter 3 on linear regression. Multiple regression is used when one dependent variable is modeled using more than one predictor at the same time. In this exercise, the TEDS2016 dataset is used to run a multiple regression model and to create regression plots showing the relationship between the dependent variable and Age, Education, and Income.

title: Assignment 3: ML Exercise
text:
2. Review ISLR Chapters 3
ISLR Chapter 3 provides the background for this assignment by explaining simple linear regression and multiple linear regression. The chapter shows that regression is used to model the relationship between a response variable and one or more predictors, and that in a multiple regression model each coefficient represents the effect of one predictor while holding the other predictors fixed.

title: Assignment 3: ML Exercise
text:
3. Load the TEDS2016 dataset
The next step is to load the TEDS2016 dataset into R using the exact code provided in the assignment. This is necessary because the dataset must be available in the R environment before the regression model and regression plots can be created.

library(haven)

TEDS_2016 <- read_stata("https://github.com/datageneration/home/blob/master/DataProgramming/data/TEDS_2016.dta?raw=true")

title: Assignment 3: ML Exercise
text:
4. Run the multiple regression model
After loading the dataset, the next step is to run a multiple regression model. Multiple regression is appropriate when the response variable is modeled using several predictors simultaneously. In this case, PartyID is used as the dependent variable, while Age, Edu, and income are used as predictors. This model estimates how each predictor is associated with the dependent variable while the other predictors are held constant.

lm.fit <- lm(PartyID ~ Age + Edu + income, data = TEDS_2016)

title: Assignment 3: ML Exercise
text:
5. Create the regplot function
The assignment then asks for a function called regplot to draw a regression fit plot. This function combines lm(), plot(), and abline() to create a scatterplot and add the fitted regression line in red. Writing the function once makes it possible to reuse the same plotting method for each predictor.

regplot=function(x,y){
 fit=lm(y~x)
 plot(x,y)
 abline(fit,col="red")
}

title: Assignment 3: ML Exercise
text:
5a. Run a regplot using Age
The first regression plot uses Age as the explanatory variable and the dependent variable as the response. This makes it possible to visually examine whether the dependent variable tends to increase or decrease as Age changes.

regplot(TEDS_2016$Age, TEDS_2016$PartyID)

title: Assignment 3: ML Exercise
text:
5b. Run a regplot using Education
The second regression plot uses Education as the explanatory variable. This plot provides a visual summary of the relationship between Education and the dependent variable and allows it to be compared with the Age plot.

regplot(TEDS_2016$Edu, TEDS_2016$PartyID)

title: Assignment 3: ML Exercise
text:
5c. Run a regplot using Income
The third regression plot uses Income as the explanatory variable. This shows whether the dependent variable appears to move upward or downward as Income changes.

regplot(TEDS_2016$income, TEDS_2016$PartyID)

title: Assignment 3: ML Exercise
text:
6. What is the problem? Why?
The main problem is that the dependent variable is not a continuous outcome. Instead, it consists of discrete categories, so the points in the regression plots appear in stacked horizontal levels rather than along a continuous scale. Because ordinary linear regression is designed for a quantitative continuous response variable, the fitted regression line is not the most appropriate way to model or predict this type of outcome.

title: Assignment 3: ML Exercise
section: 7. What can be done to improve prediction of the dependent variable?
text:
7. What can be done to improve prediction of the dependent variable?
Prediction can be improved by using a model that is designed for a categorical dependent variable rather than ordinary linear regression. A better choice would be multinomial logistic regression if the dependent variable has several categories. Another possible improvement would be to recode the dependent variable into fewer meaningful groups before modeling.

text:
17.1 Intertopic Map Overview
This section is separate from the earlier graphs because it uses topic modeling rather than simple word-frequency analysis. The goal is to uncover broader themes in the breach descriptions and visualize how similar or different those themes are from one another.
The labels shown on the map are researcher-assigned summaries based on each topic’s most defining words. This means the model identifies the word patterns first, and the final topic labels are then interpreted in plain language.

17.3 Step 2: Trim the Document-Feature Matrix for Topic Modeling
This step creates a version of the document-feature matrix specifically for topic modeling. Very rare terms and overly common terms are trimmed so that the model focuses on words that are more useful for identifying themes.

dfmat_topic <- quanteda::dfm_trim(
  dfmat,
  min_termfreq = 5,
  min_docfreq = 2,
  max_docfreq = floor(quanteda::ndoc(dfmat) * 0.85),
  docfreq_type = "count"
)

if (quanteda::nfeat(dfmat_topic) < 10) {
  stop("Too few terms remain after trimming for topic modeling. Lower min_termfreq or min_docfreq and try again.")
}

cat("Topic-modeling DFM:", quanteda::ndoc(dfmat_topic), "documents and", quanteda::nfeat(dfmat_topic), "features\n")

text:
17.4 Step 3: Convert the Matrix and Fit the LDA Model
This step converts the quanteda matrix into the format required by topicmodels, then fits a Latent Dirichlet Allocation model. The model is set to estimate five topics.

dtm_topic <- quanteda::convert(dfmat_topic, to = "topicmodels")

set.seed(1234)
k <- 5

lda_fit <- topicmodels::LDA(
  dtm_topic,
  k = k,
  control = list(seed = 1234)
)

lda_fit

A LDA_VEM topic model with 5 topics.

17.5 Step 4: Extract Topic-Term and Document-Topic Probabilities
This step pulls out the two main outputs of the topic model:

phi: the probability of each term within each topic
theta: the probability of each topic within each document

These are the core parts for labeling topics and building the intertopic map.

post <- topicmodels::posterior(lda_fit)

phi <- post$terms
theta <- post$topics

text:
17.10 Step 9: Calculate Dominant Topic Share
This step calculates the share of documents assigned most strongly to each topic.
This makes topic prevalence easier to interpret than simply averaging topic probabilities, which can look artificially even across topics.

dominant_topic <- apply(theta, 1, which.max)

topic_prevalence <- round(
  100 * prop.table(table(factor(dominant_topic, levels = 1:k))),
  1
)

topic_prevalence <- as.numeric(topic_prevalence)

prevalence_df <- tibble::tibble(
  topic_id = 1:k,
  prevalence_percent = topic_prevalence
)

knitr::kable(
  prevalence_df,
  caption = "Dominant topic share across the corpus"

section: 17.12 Step 11: Create the Interactive Intertopic Map
text:
17.12 Step 11: Create the Interactive Intertopic Map
This is the final visualization step. Each bubble is a topic, the size reflects prevalence, the placement reflects similarity to other topics, and the hover text shows the topic meaning and top defining words.

bubble_sizes <- scales::rescale(as.numeric(topic_map$prevalence), to = c(35, 90))

plotly::plot_ly(
  data = topic_map,
  x = ~x,
  y = ~y,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers+text",
  text = ~label,
  textposition = "top center",
  hovertemplate = ~paste0(
    "<b>", label, "</b><br>",
    "Dominant-topic share: ", prevalence, "%<br>",
    "Top terms: ", top_terms, "<br>",
    "Meaning: ", meaning,
    "<extra></extra>"
  ),
  marker = list(
    size = bubble_sizes,
    color = topic_map$color,
    opacity = 0.80,
    line = list(color = "#8a0f4d", width = 1.5)
  )
) %>%
  plotly::layout(
    title = list(text = "Interactive Intertopic Distance Map"),
    xaxis = list(title = "Dimension 1"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Dimension 2")
  )

title: CYBER INSURANCE IN HEALTHCARE RESEARCH
text:
17.13 What the Output Means
The intertopic map should be read as a visual summary of how the latent topics relate to one another. If two bubbles are close together, that means those topics use similar vocabulary and are thematically related. If two bubbles are farther apart, that means their word distributions are more distinct.
Bubble size reflects dominant-topic share. A larger bubble means that topic is the main theme in more documents, while a smaller bubble means it is dominant in fewer documents.
The words shown in the hover text are the highest-probability terms for that topic.
These are the terms that most strongly define the topic according to the model.
The topic names are interpretive labels assigned after inspecting those top words.
In other words, the model discovers the word patterns first, and the final topic name is the human-readable explanation of what that pattern appears to represent.

title: CYBER INSURANCE IN HEALTHCARE RESEARCH
text:
17.14 Topic Modeling Notes
This section differs from the earlier graphs because it does not simply count words or categories. Instead, it uses co-occurrence patterns across documents to estimate latent topics, which can reveal broader thematic structure in the breach narratives.
